newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy brings crisis bid to embattled Israel.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy brings crisis bid to embattled Israel.

text.p: U.S. presidential envoy Dennis Ross is to meet Israeli leaders on Friday in an urgent bid to quell a crisis threatening to send hard-won Israeli-PLO accords up in flames.

As Ross held overnight talks on Thursday with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, thousands of Israeli soldiers and police, backed by tanks and helicopters, girded for the possibility of violent Palestinian protests over construction of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
The envoy was to hold talks on Friday with Netanyahu, Foreign Minister David Levy, and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai.
Ross arrived late on Thursday after talks in Morocco with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. President Bill Clinton said the Ross-Arafat talks were encouraging, but did not elaborate.
Last week Netanyahu's hardline government sent bulldozers to break ground for the settlement, plunging ties with the PLO into turmoil and unleashing Palestinian rage in daily unrest.

The crisis deepened last Friday, when a Palestinian suicide bomber walked into a Tel Aviv cafe, blowing himself up and killing three women. Israel charges Arafat had effectively given a "green light" for the bloodshed.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called on Arafat to give a "red light" to stop guerrilla attacks against Israel.
Palestinians counter that Israel spawned the violence by starting work on thousands of homes for Jews in East Jerusalem, seen by Arabs as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
Arafat called the work "a crime against the peace process."
Clashes spurred by the settlement entered an eighth day on Thursday. About 200 Arabs near Ramallah hurled stones at Israeli troops, who responded with rubber bullets and tear gas.
In wave after wave of past crises, Ross has proven a dogged engineer of peacemaking, bridging seemingly yawning gaps.

But analysts have called the settlement row as tough a test for Ross as a fierce flare-up months ago when, in the wake of gun battles that killed 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis, the envoy brokered Israel's handover of most of Hebron to self-rule.

They said Ross could devise a formula by which Arafat would recommit himself to fight violence and Netanyahu would promise not to take any more unilateral steps such as last week's ground-breaking on the Jewish settlement.
Publicly, however, Israeli officials have maintained there can be no Israeli gestures until Arafat cracks down on violence.
Israeli security chiefs have warned of a potential surge of unrest climaxing on Sunday -- the annual "Land Day" when Israeli Arabs stage protests against government confiscation of lands.
Israeli army chief Amnon Shahak, saying he hoped the weekend would pass calmly, told reporters: "There's no lack of tanks... The problem isn't tanks. The problem is how not to use force."
Police officials said reinforcements would take up positions near Moslem prayer sites in Jerusalem's Old City and near the settlement site in pre-dawn hours on Friday.
"Police forces will act with vehemence and determination, and head off all attempts to violate law and order," said police spokesman Shmulik Ben-Ruby.

Palestinians urged Ross to lean on Israel to halt work on the East Jerusalem hilltop settlement which the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim and the Israelis call Har Homa. In a move largely unrecognised internationally, Israel annexed East Jerusalem after capturing it in the 1967 Middle East War.
Israel Television's Channel One unveiled another new settlement on Thursday, showing film of a small enclave in the West Bank near Ramallah.
Ross has said he would return to Washington by the weekend to report to Clinton so the "president can decide what the next proper move should be".
